name: Entity Framework Core
summary: Microsoft’s object-relational mapper for .NET: you query C# classes with LINQ, a `DbContext` tracks the entities it loads, and `SaveChanges` writes every change back as SQL through a pluggable database provider.
intro: An EF Core model is a set of entity classes plus a context class derived from `DbContext`, with a `DbSet<T>` property per table. You can write the classes first and let EF Migrations create and evolve the database, or generate the model from an existing database. Queries are LINQ expressions (`db.Blogs.Where(b => b.Rating > 3).ToListAsync()`) that the provider translates to SQL. Every entity a query returns, or that you `Add` or `Attach`, is tracked by the context’s change tracker; `SaveChanges` turns the tracked changes into `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` statements. A `DbContext` is meant to be a short-lived unit of work: create it, load, change, save, dispose.

Related data is loaded eagerly with `Include`, explicitly, or lazily through an optional proxies package or an injected loader. Microsoft’s performance guide recommends avoiding lazy loading because it makes the N+1 problem easy to trigger. When LINQ can’t express a query, `FromSql` starts a query from raw SQL. Databases plug in as providers: Microsoft ships SQL Server and Azure SQL, SQLite and Azure Cosmos DB, while PostgreSQL (Npgsql), MySQL and MariaDB (Pomelo, or Oracle’s own) and others come from third parties. EF Core is released with each .NET version: EF Core 10, a long-term support release from November 2025, is supported until November 2028, and EF Core 11 is planned for November 2026.
strengths: LINQ queries checked by the C# compiler, translated to readable SQL
Change tracking and `SaveChanges` give a unit of work for free in short-lived contexts
Migrations, scaffolding from an existing database and a provider model covering SQL Server, SQLite, Cosmos DB, PostgreSQL, MySQL and more
Shipped and supported by Microsoft on the .NET release cadence, with long-term support releases
limits: LINQ hides the SQL: an innocent-looking query can produce a slow plan or N+1 round trips unless you log and check the generated SQL
Lazy loading is opt-in but, once on, makes the N+1 problem easy to trigger
Provider quality varies: PostgreSQL and MySQL support comes from third-party projects with their own release timing
Not every EF6 feature came over: the graphical model designer and EDMX files are not planned, and updating a model from a changed database is still on the backlog

snippet.title: Load blogs with their posts in one query, change one, and save
source: await using var db = new BloggingContext();   // a DbContext with DbSet<Blog> Blogs
// Include loads the posts with the blogs instead of one query per blog later
await db.SaveChangesAsync();                 // one UPDATE for the changed row

story: Microsoft’s first object-relational mapper for .NET was the ADO.NET Entity Framework, shipped with .NET Framework 3.5 Service Pack 1 and Visual Studio 2008 SP1 on 11 August 2008. It was widely criticised: a “vote of no confidence” from developers experienced with entity-based architectures gathered at least a thousand signatures. Version 4.0 in 2010 answered many of the complaints, 4.1 in 2011 added Code First, and Entity Framework 6 in 2013 became open source under the Apache License.

When Microsoft rebuilt .NET as a cross-platform, modular runtime, it rewrote the ORM too. The new version was first called Entity Framework 7; in January 2016 Microsoft renamed it Entity Framework Core 1.0, alongside .NET Core 1.0 and ASP.NET Core 1.0, because it was a new product rather than an upgrade. EF Core 1.0 shipped on 27 June 2016 as a “lightweight, extensible, and cross-platform version of Entity Framework”, without every EF6 feature.

Since then EF Core has shipped with each .NET release and caught up on most of EF6: lazy loading in 2.1, table-per-type inheritance and many-to-many without a join class in 5.0, table-per-concrete-type and custom conventions in 7.0. EF6 is still supported but no longer actively developed.

choices.choice: A rewrite instead of porting EF6
choices.why: EF6 was built for the Windows-only .NET Framework. A lightweight, extensible core that ran on .NET Core across platforms meant starting again, and accepting that some EF6 features would arrive late or never.
A provider model let SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Cosmos DB and other teams ship support themselves instead of waiting for Microsoft to build each one.

choices.choice: Short-lived contexts as the unit of work
choices.why: Each `DbContext` tracks the entities it loaded and writes their changes at `SaveChanges`, so a web request maps naturally to one context and one transaction.

EF Core 1.0 shipped without lazy loading. Version 2.1 added the building blocks plus an optional proxies package, and Microsoft still recommends eager or explicit loading because they make each database round trip visible in the code.

timeline.text: Entity Framework 1 ships with .NET Framework 3.5 SP1
Entity Framework 6 is released as open source
EF7 is renamed EF Core 1.0 in January; 1.0 ships on 27 June
EF Core 5.0 adds table-per-type inheritance and many-to-many
EF Core 10 ships in November as a long-term support release
